name: MALI
lead: Mali is a vast landlocked country where the Niger River curves across the Sahara's edge. Once home to the world's richest empires, kings here gave away gold as gifts. Today mud-brick mosques rise like sandcastles, nomads ride camels across golden dunes, and griots keep ancient tales alive with kora harps and talking drums.
geo: Mali is two-thirds Sahara Desert — an ocean of golden sand where temperatures soar above 45 °C. The Niger River is its lifeline, flooding farmland each year and feeding millions with fish and rice.

The Sahel grassland belt runs across the south, turning green after rains. The Bandiagara Cliffs rise 500 m from the plain, where Dogon people have carved cliff-side villages into rock for nearly a thousand years.
animals: The Niger River shelters hippos and Nile crocodiles that bask on sandy banks. African manatees glide through quiet backwaters — slow, whiskered mammals rarely seen elsewhere in West Africa.

Desert-adapted creatures roam the north: fennec foxes with enormous ears, sand gazelles, and golden jackals. Rare West African giraffes still wander near the Niger's inland delta, stretching tall to reach acacia leaves.
culture: Mali is the birthplace of the griot — musician, historian and storyteller in one. Griots play the kora (a 21-string harp-lute made from a gourd) and recite royal histories going back 700 years.

The Great Mosque of Djenné is the world's largest mud-brick building, replastered by the whole town after every rainy season. Malian mud cloth (bogolanfini) is hand-painted with symbols that tell stories in pattern and colour.
history: Around 1300 CE the Mali Empire ruled territory bigger than Western Europe. Emperor Mansa Musa was possibly history's wealthiest person — his 1324 pilgrimage with 12,000 servants and tonnes of gold caused inflation across North Africa.
Timbuktu became a great centre of learning with over 25,000 university students. Mali gained independence from France on 22 September 1960, celebrated today as its national holiday.
wows: The Great Mosque of Djenné has been replastered from mud every year for over 800 years.
Mansa Musa's 1324 caravan had 60,000 people and carried roughly 18 tonnes of gold.
Mali holds over 700,000 ancient manuscripts, some stored in family homes in Timbuktu.
The Niger Inland Delta floods yearly into a wetland the size of Belgium, drawing millions of birds.
Timbuktu was so legendary that Europeans offered prizes to whoever could reach it and return.
Malian guitarist Ali Farka Touré's style directly shaped American blues music history.
Dogon people described the invisible star Sirius B centuries before telescopes confirmed it.

myths.fact: Only two-thirds is desert; the south has rivers, forests, farmland and wetlands hosting dramatic wildlife migrations.
Timbuktu was one of the medieval world's great cities — a wealthy trading hub with 180 Quranic schools at its peak.
